data.title: Hatné – two small hillforts in the Marikovská valley
data.excerpt: North of the village of Hatné, two small fortifications face each other across the Marikovský stream in the locality known as Hrádok, and Štefan Janšák described them in 1930. The Väčší hrádok was fortified by the people of the Baden culture as early as the 3rd millennium BC, while the Menší hrádok has been almost entirely taken apart by local people.
data.metaTitle: Hatné – two small hillforts in the Marikovská valley
data.metaDescription: Two small fortifications at Hrádok near Hatné document one of the oldest occupations of the Marikovská valley; Štefan Janšák described them in 1930.

children.text: North of the village of Hatné, on both sides of the Marikovský stream, in the locality known as Hrádok, there are two smaller fortifications which document one of the oldest occupations in the whole of the Marikovská valley. Štefan Janšák wrote the following about them in 1930:

blocks.text: In the Marikovská valley, about one third of the way between the villages of Hátne and Maríková, two remarkable rocky spurs rise facing each other, one on each side of the brook. They approach each other to within a distance of 80 m, by which a narrow pass is created in the valley, barely sufficient for the little brook with its flat gravelly bed and for a vicinal road of a width and quality adapted all too well to its poor surroundings. The situation of the two crags is so unusual that it worked even upon the imagination of the people, who placed upon them two old castles, once joined by a leather bridge. In the immediate neighbourhood of the eastern hrádok, which we shall name the ‘Larger’, stands a chapel with a cemetery, and at its southern foot a wooden cross.

blocks.caption: The romantic notion of the two hrádky linked by a leather bridge is based on a legend already recorded at the end of the 19th century. Janšák noted it down as well in 1930 (by Tomáš Humaj)
blocks.alt: The romantic notion of the two hrádky linked by a leather bridge is based on a legend already recorded at the end of the 19th century. Janšák noted it down as well in 1930 (by Tomáš Humaj)

children.text: The Väčší hrádok (the Larger) is a typical example of a hillfort built on a rocky promontory projecting into the valley. The hrádok is not only better preserved than the one opposite, but the occupation here is also much older. It goes back as far as the 3rd millennium BC, when the people of the Baden culture settled here. It was enough for the inhabitants of the hillfort to dig the ditch J k, 3 m deep, and to use the material obtained to build the rampart a b, in order to create a safe enclosure of the surface plateau. In this case nature met the first inhabitants with unusual kindness. On three sides the plateau is protected by a vertical rock on average 20 m high. Only on the north-east and the north was there free access along the ridge, barred by the arc-shaped rampart a b, 36 m long, 5 m high towards the outside and 2 m towards the inside. Its continuation is formed by the low rampart c d, 18 m long, today barely perceptible.

The surface of the hillfort, with an area of 1,970 m², offers all the advantages of a small settlement. It lies on the southern slope of a massif falling away into the valley and is thus protected against the cold winds. In addition, the artificial rampart a b directly shelters the belt adjoining it and exposes its southern slope to the sun. The water indispensable for the life of the inhabitants is to be found in the immediate vicinity. The modest area does not permit an alternation of several fortified enclosures, and the hard rock subsoil prevents the building of other installations needed for habitation.

blocks.caption: An artist's impression of the appearance of the medieval hrádok of the Hatňanský family. (author: Bohuš Šikulínec)
blocks.alt: An artist's impression of the appearance of the medieval hrádok of the Hatňanský family. (author: Bohuš Šikulínec)

children.text:
The Menší hrádok (the Smaller), lying 80 m west of the previous one on the right bank of the Marikovka, perhaps deserves this name only today. The inhabitants of the surrounding villages and kopanice (scattered hill farmsteads) have already taken apart almost the whole of the limestone rock of which it is composed, leaving only two sharp pinnacles of differing height. The Menší hrádok must certainly have had a more glorious past than its neighbour; it was evidently stronger and also richer. By a remarkable freak of nature a rock cone 20 m high arose here with a summit plateau that is small, it is true, but comfortable. It needed no work at all to become a safe place of refuge, except perhaps for primitive steps cut into the rock leading to its summit. Of its former strength and might only a skeleton remains today, two rocky arms stretched out to heaven as if begging for mercy. That is why the cartographer could record and immortalise nothing of it either, leaving this task to the photographic plate. That the Menší hrádok was once the Larger is testified by the considerably greater quantity of sherds found at its foot and in the fields extending westwards from it. The finds here are richer and more varied than in the previous case. Coarse-grained, poorly fired sherds predominate. One of the fragments of a vessel has a great deal of graphite admixed.
On both hrádky fine-grained sherds were found, black on the surface and at the fracture, weakly fired. The admixture is not graphite but certainly charcoal powder, which can be detected in at least 50% of the Hallstatt, La Tène and hillfort-period sherds that were found. Where the vessels were perfectly fired it has disappeared completely and there is no trace of it. In less well fired ones a dark layer remains at the fracture; in those fired very little, the surface too is black.

A continuation of the occupation in the following period we do not yet have attested; it is documented only from the Final Bronze Age and the beginning of the Early Iron Age. At that time not only the Hrádok crag itself was occupied but also the area beside it, where a settlement of the people of the Lusatian culture arose. Štefan Janšák found here sherds of the Hallstatt period and a grinding stone of quartzite sandstone with a maximum grain size of 1 mm.

blocks.caption: Janšák dates the grinding stone to the Hallstatt period
blocks.alt: Janšák dates the grinding stone to the Hallstatt period

children.text: At the turn of the eras the Hrádok on the right side of the stream was fortified as well; sadly it has by now been so destroyed by stone quarrying that only a torso of it remains. In the immediate vicinity of this fortification there was also a settlement of the people of the Púchov culture, where fragments of vessels, stone whetstones and pieces of burnt daub from the rendering of the walls of wooden dwellings were found.

The continuation of the occupation is then interrupted for almost a thousand years, because the Slavic population did not settle here until the 9th century AD. It lasted only a short time, but since the Slavs gradually took possession of the whole territory of northern Slovakia, it was only a matter of time before a medieval village arose here too.

Jozef Moravčík states that the medieval finds (14th–15th century) from the Hrádok on the right side of the stream indicate that there was evidently a fortification here of the local landlord, who in the 15th century became the owner of Budatín Castle. Juraj z Hatného obtained Budatín from King Sigismund for his loyal services. His first known ancestor, Kilián, had already received Hatné, Prosné and Mariková from King Charles Robert in 1321.

Probably already at that time he built his residence here — a medieval hrádok which served his descendants as well, until they became the owners of a more important fortress, Budatín. We know neither the original extent nor the appearance of the hrádok, because a substantial part of it was destroyed by a quarry. And so about its history only the written records and the medieval sherds found here now tell us. It has been confirmed once again that ill-considered interference with the terrain considerably impoverishes our knowledge of our distant past, when important features are destroyed whose investigation could have brought weighty evidence not only for understanding the history of the village concerned but also in a wider context.

blocks.caption: Two very fine visualisations of the hillforts were created for us by Antonín Lacko
blocks.alt: Two very fine visualisations of the hillforts were created for us by Antonín Lacko

children.text: In the 15th century another important feudal lord of the Hatňanský family, who perhaps resided at the hrádok, was Juraj z Hatného, of whom we know that in 1436 he received Budatín Castle as a property from Sigismund of Luxembourg. The fate of both hrádky was sealed by the quarry, which completely destroyed one of the sites and considerably damaged the other. Both have been declared archaeological sites. In the village a story is handed down about a leather bridge connecting the hrádky, which is contradicted by the finds, which show that the hrádky were not occupied at the same time in any of the periods. A connection by a bridge is therefore unlikely.
